correctness.rationale: Verified the all-phase claim analytically. Under inverse ellipse scaling, area maximization reduces to maximizing the sum of sines of the cyclic gaps. On the compact space with nonnegative gaps, a coincident-vertex polygon is not a maximizer: insertion on an open boundary arc makes a positive-area addition for a polygon with ≥3 distinct vertices, or yields positive area starting with ≤2. At an interior maximum the adjacent two-gap sine identity makes each adjacent gap pair equal. For the resulting equal-angle family the moving-vertex tangent is the average of the two unnormalized chord directions divided by cos(h); dotting it with the difference of incident unit chord vectors gives D_j=(F⁻−F⁺)(1−cos θ)/(2 cos h). The determinant ab sin(2h) makes the second factor strictly positive, and the squared norm difference is −(a²−b²)sin(2h)sin(2t_j). Thus simultaneous vanishing requires n=4 and a vertex phase in (π/2)Z. The grid modulo π gives max |sin(2t_j)|≥cos(π/(2N)); F⁻+F⁺≤2a and 1−cos θ≥sin²θ/2 give the stated G. Moving a single angle by up to h preserves order and gives incident gaps in [h,3h]⊂[h,π], so chord norms are at least 2b sin(h/2). The twice-differentiated norm bound then gives precisely H and the Taylor increment ≥G min(h,G/H)/2. Compactness gives a maximum; a collapsed polygon can strictly increase perimeter by insertion by strict triangle inequality, so an actual distinct-vertex maximum exists. The tests were inspected as diagnostics, not executed or used as a continuum proof. No claim of global maximality at n=4.
